item_name: Emergency Brake System (EBS) Design Approaches for Formula Student Driverless
competition_series: Applies across FSG, FSAE (incl. FSAE-A), FS UK, FS Czech, FS East and other FSAE-derived driverless rulesets - all require an EBS meeting an equivalent of FSAE DT.3.2 / historical T15.2, and an equivalent of the DI.2 (formerly T15/DV3.3) dynamic Emergency Brake Test.
summary: Across the Formula Student driverless corpus reviewed (KTH, Politecnico di Torino/Squadra Corse, Chalmers, the official FSG Autonomous System Beginners Guide reference design, and the FSAE Driverless Systems Form example), three EBS architectures recur: (1) direct pneumatic actuation of the existing hydraulic brake pedal or an added master cylinder via a compressed-air/CO2 cylinder and 3/2 solenoid valve; (2) a pneumo-hydraulic intensifier hybrid - the most fully documented and apparently most common approach - where a certified compressed-air tank drives a custom pressure intensifier that produces 40-70 bar hydraulic pressure into duplicated brake lines via shuttle valves; and (3) a rarer electromechanical/spring-based 'removal of counterforce' design, described in the FSG reference guide but not found fully implemented in any publicly available thesis in this research pass. Every documented design exploits the vehicle's pre-existing hydraulic service-brake hardware (master cylinder, calipers, balance bar) rather than building a stand-alone brake circuit, which is a hard prerequisite: no EBS design in this corpus starts from scratch. Concrete cost, lead-time, and full concept-to-passing-test duration data are rarely published by teams; the richest quantitative source found is a 2019-2020 Politecnico di Torino thesis pair (design study + build-and-bench-test study) that gives real per-component costs (e.g. shuttle/OR valves at EUR 100 vs EUR 420 each) and bench-test results, but even that pair stops short of a full on-vehicle DI.2 pass, illustrating how the corpus consistently under-reports the final integration-and-test phase. Steering actuation content is covered in a companion item (Steering Actuation Approaches for Driverless) and is summarized only briefly here.
evidence_quality: moderate: strong primary-source detail (full master's theses, official FSG/SAE reference documents with real part numbers) exists for EBS mechanical architecture, force/actuation-time sizing calculations, and component-level costs from a small number of teams (mainly KTH and Politecnico di Torino/Squadra Corse); but cross-team aggregation of total program cost, procurement lead times in weeks, iteration counts, and concept-to-passing-EBS-test duration is thin - most teams (Chalmers, DUT, EUFS, Monash, QUT, TUfast, e-gnition, UTFR per prior research passes in this project) do not publish these numbers at all, so those figures here are synthesized/estimated from component class and sourcing channel and are flagged [uncertain].
months_concept_to_first_autonomous_run: [uncertain] Repurposed as: typical months from EBS subsystem concept to a bench-validated (rig-tested, not yet vehicle-integrated) EBS. Evidence points to roughly 6-9 months for a single academic-year thesis cycle covering concept through bench validation (KTH thesis: 'approximately 6-9 months of formal thesis work... building on earlier informal concept work', defended 27 June 2018; Politecnico di Torino thesis webthesis.biblio.polito.it/16284: one academic year, 2019-2020, concept through successful bench-test validation of pressure build-up, single-line-failure behaviour, and full-mission state-machine simulation, but explicitly not yet vehicle-mounted at thesis submission). Sample size is very small (2-3 documented cases), so treat this as an order-of-magnitude estimate, not a benchmark.
months_concept_to_first_competition: [uncertain] Repurposed as: typical months from EBS concept to a first attempt at the EBS dynamic test (DI.2-equivalent) at a competition. No source in this pass gives a clean single-team concept-to-first-attempt number; the closest proxy is Politecnico di Torino/Squadra Corse's EBS work spanning two consecutive thesis cycles (Danese, AY2019-2020, bench-validated only, and a later design-only follow-on thesis AY2020-2021 that explicitly restarts much of the sizing work for a different actuation approach), implying the full concept-to-first-competition-attempt cycle commonly runs longer than a single ~9-month thesis, plausibly 12-18 months when vehicle integration and initial test-day iteration are included.
months_to_first_scoring_run: [uncertain] Repurposed as: typical months from EBS concept to first PASSING EBS test / first scored driverless dynamic event. No team in this corpus published a clean concept-to-first-pass number. Adjacent evidence from this project's team-level research (not this item's own primary sources, cited for context only): University of Toronto Formula Racing documented roughly 6 months between standalone EBS subsystem validation (Nov 2023) and full vehicle implementation (May 2024); QUT Motorsport's EBS-mission control logic existed by mid-2022 but the system was still being re-tuned through at least Dec 2024/Jan 2026, i.e. multi-year maturation to a fully competition-reliable state. Best estimate: 12-24 months from EBS concept to a first pass of the EBS dynamic test, with wide variance driven by how many hardware iterations and how much CI/scrutineering-day retesting is required.

year_by_year_timeline.mechanical_focus: Read DT.3.1/DT.3.2 and DSF.5 (Pressure System Overview) requirements; decide pneumatic vs. pneumo-hydraulic-intensifier vs. electromechanical architecture based on whether an existing hydraulic service-brake system can be leveraged (almost always yes for an EV conversion).
year_by_year_timeline.electrical_focus: Define EBS relay/redundant-EBS-relay power-stage topology per the FSG reference (direct, no-delay supply from GLVMS/DSMS/Remote Stop Relay/EBS Relay).
year_by_year_timeline.software_focus: Draft the EBS Supervisor state machine (Startup Check, continuous monitoring, actuation, release) at a spec level.
year_by_year_timeline.milestone_achieved: Architecture selection and force/pressure sizing calculations (e.g. static brake pedal force, actuation-time load-factor derating).

year_by_year_timeline.mechanical_focus: Detail-design pneumatic/hydraulic circuit (tanks, valves, intensifiers or direct actuators, shuttle valves, brackets); source certified pressure tank/regulator (long lead).
year_by_year_timeline.electrical_focus: Select and procure solenoid valves, pressure sensors, relays, MOSFET power stages.
year_by_year_timeline.software_focus: Implement EBS Supervisor logic on target hardware; simulate full-mission arm/check/actuate/release cycle before hardware is connected.
year_by_year_timeline.milestone_achieved: First fabricated components; software-in-the-loop simulation of the EBS sequence passes.

year_by_year_timeline.mechanical_focus: Assemble sub-systems on a bench rig; validate pressure build-up, single-line-failure half-performance, and repeated-actuation endurance (e.g. a 200 bar canister supporting 30+ actuations before refill in one documented case).
year_by_year_timeline.electrical_focus: Validate Startup Check watchdog routine and continuous monitoring thresholds on the bench.
year_by_year_timeline.software_focus: Validate EBS Supervisor state transitions against bench hardware; log and analyze via CAN/DBC.
year_by_year_timeline.milestone_achieved: Bench-validated EBS meeting design pressure/force targets (documented example: pneumo-hydraulic intensifier design reaching ~40 bar full-line / ~20 bar single-line-failure hydraulic pressure on the bench).

year_by_year_timeline.mechanical_focus: Install on vehicle, integrate with existing hydraulic lines without disturbing brake balance (balance bar), verify Deactivation Point placement/marking per DT.3.1.2.
year_by_year_timeline.electrical_focus: Integrate EBS relay chain into full vehicle Shutdown Circuit; verify no-delay behaviour end-to-end.
year_by_year_timeline.software_focus: Progressive on-vehicle testing: static (jacked-up) full-sequence test, then low-speed dynamic tests building to the full ~40 km/h DI.2 profile.
year_by_year_timeline.milestone_achieved: First on-vehicle dynamic EBS actuation; iterate through scrutineering EBS-test attempts (multiple attempts/requeues are commonly needed per the FSG reference guide's own framing).
year_by_year_timeline.competition_result: N/A - this item is not a team and has no competition results.

ramp_phases: Named phases observed/synthesized across sources: (1) 'Rules study & architecture selection' 2-4 weeks; (2) 'Sizing & CAD' 4-8 weeks; (3) 'Component sourcing', gated by certified-tank/custom-intensifier lead times, 4-10 weeks and often run in parallel with (2); (4) 'Fabrication & bench-rig build' 4-8 weeks; (5) 'Bench validation' (Startup Check routine, redundancy/single-line-failure tests, endurance/actuation-count tests) 4-8 weeks; (6) 'Vehicle integration' 4-12 weeks; (7) 'Dynamic test iteration' at scrutineering, open-ended (FSG guide explicitly plans for teams needing to 'requeue' if a test run is unsuccessful or too slow).
what_slipped: Common EBS-specific schedule slips found in this corpus: (1) the Politecnico di Torino design-only thesis (webthesis.biblio.polito.it/18714) reached a complete, FEM-validated design but explicitly left fabrication and vehicle testing as 'way forward' - i.e. the design phase alone consumed the available thesis time, slipping build/test to a later cycle; (2) the companion implementation thesis (webthesis.biblio.polito.it/16284) completed component and subassembly bench testing successfully but explicitly still needed hydraulic-line completion, vehicle mounting, pedal-assembly connection, and full-vehicle testing beyond the thesis timeframe; (3) KTH's ISO 26262 safety analysis identified that full compliance would require an additional CPU and extensive signal-verification redundancy, but the team chose NOT to implement these due to 'limited resources in terms of money and time' - a scope-cut rather than a schedule slip, but driven by the same resource constraints; (4) Chalmers' original pneumatic-clamp linear steering actuator design (adjacent subsystem, same 2019 thesis) was found post-hoc to have a play/backlash defect causing measurable steering-angle error, discovered only after a season of use rather than caught in bench validation - a validation-strategy gap, not a scheduling one, but it forced a redesign recommendation.
platform_prerequisites: N/A as a team-history field, but functionally significant: every EBS design found in this corpus (KTH, Politecnico di Torino/Squadra Corse SC19, the FSG reference design) is built as an add-on that actuates the vehicle's PRE-EXISTING hydraulic service-brake system (master cylinder(s), calipers, balance bar) rather than a stand-alone brake circuit. A working, already-tuned hydraulic brake system (i.e. a completed EV/IC car) is therefore a hard prerequisite before EBS mechanical design can meaningfully start, since actuator force/stroke sizing is derived directly from the existing pedal-box geometry and required line pressures.
ebs_design:
Three architectures recur across sources, all satisfying DT.3.2.1.a (passive mechanical energy storage only) and DT.3.2.1.b (direct, no-delay supply from GLVMS/DSMS/Remote Stop Relay/EBS Relay):

1) DIRECT PNEUMATIC ACTUATION (KTH; FSG reference guide Figures 13-15): a CO2 gas cartridge or compressed-air cylinder pressurizes a pneumatic cylinder through a normally-open 3/2 solenoid valve; brakes are held OFF only while the valve is electrically energized, so power loss vents the valve and dumps stored pressure into the actuator (passive-by-default). Three connection options to the existing brake system are documented: (a) actuator directly on the brake pedal (simplest, but must avoid blocking manual pedal travel and avoid lateral-force introduction into the pneumatic cylinder - anti-blocking slots or swivel mounts required); (b) actuator on a second/added master cylinder combined via a shuttle (OR) valve into the existing circuit (more cockpit-space-friendly, allows independent front/rear pressure tuning); (c) actuator on a self-built combined pneumatic/hydraulic pressure transducer (highest failure risk per the FSG guide, 'only if you exactly know what you are doing').

2) PNEUMO-HYDRAULIC INTENSIFIER HYBRID (Politecnico di Torino/Squadra Corse SC19, both theses reviewed; the FSAE Driverless Systems Form example BOM): a certified compressed-air tank (example: Protoyz 0.8 L aluminium, 200 bar max, PI-certified) is regulated down (example: Tescom BB-13AL3KEA regulator, 414 bar input rating, 0-15.2 bar output range) and fed through solenoid valves (example: FESTO MHE2-M1H-3/2O-M7, 8 bar max) into small buffer tanks (example: FESTO CRVZS-0.4, 16 bar max), which drive a custom pneumatic-to-hydraulic pressure intensifier converting ~10 bar air into ~40-70 bar hydraulic oil; hydraulic output merges with the driver's existing master-cylinder line via a shuttle/OR valve (example: AP Racing CP5088-1, or a custom Fluido Sistem valve) before reaching the calipers (example: AP Racing CP4227-2S0). Two fully independent front/rear lines are duplicated end-to-end (tank, valve, sensor, intensifier, shuttle valve) to satisfy DT.3.2.5.c half-performance-on-single-failure; bench testing of one documented implementation showed ~40 bar with both lines working and ~20 bar (roughly half) with only one line triggered, directly demonstrating the required single-failure behaviour.

3) ELECTROMECHANICAL / SPRING 'REMOVAL OF COUNTERFORCE' (described in the FSG Autonomous System Beginners Guide Section 9.4-9.5 as a valid passive-energy-storage option; not found fully implemented in any thesis reviewed): brakes are held permanently pre-loaded by redundant springs; releasing the brakes for normal driving requires continuously applying a counter-force (electrically, e.g. via a solenoid or motor holding tension) or a released pneumatic counter-pressure; loss of that counter-force/pressure is itself the passive EBS trigger. Advantage: avoids pressure-vessel certification/5-year-expiry burden entirely. Disadvantage: continuous power draw to hold brakes off, and a mechanical detent/latch is needed for manual driving mode. One team in this project's broader research (QUT, per prior team-level research) describes a 2023 'new emergency brake actuator' as ambiguously 'electromechanical/pneumatic' without public detail, so this architecture may be more common in practice than the published-thesis corpus suggests - flagged [uncertain]. For steering actuator detail (a separate DT.2 subsystem) see the companion item 'Steering Actuation Approaches for Driverless'.
ebs_development_duration: See months_concept_to_first_autonomous_run/months_to_first_scoring_run above for the synthesized cross-team estimate (~6-9 months concept-to-bench-validated, ~12-24 months concept-to-first-competition-pass). [uncertain] Only two teams in the corpus give any duration figure at all, and neither completes the full cycle within their documented thesis: Politecnico di Torino's design-only thesis (18714) covers concept through FEM-validated design in roughly one academic year (2020-2021) without reaching fabrication; the companion implementation thesis (16284) covers concept through successful bench validation in roughly one academic year (2019-2020, AY2019/2020) without reaching full vehicle testing.
ebs_cost_estimate: [uncertain] No team in this corpus published a single total EBS program cost. The best sourced data point is Politecnico di Torino's shuttle/OR-valve trade study (thesis 16284): a Fluido Sistem valve at EUR 100/each versus a The Lee Company valve at EUR 420/each (lower weight/size but ~4x cost; team chose the cheaper, heavier option), plus generic pneumatic/hydraulic fittings quoted at 'less than EUR 10 each'. Building a rough purchased-component BOM estimate from the FSAE Driverless Systems Form example architecture and general industrial/motorsport catalog pricing knowledge (NOT from a single sourced total, so treat as a synthesized estimate): 2x solenoid valves (~USD 60-120 each), 2x small buffer tanks (~USD 40-80 each), 2x pressure sensors (~USD 150-250 each), a supply-side regulator (~USD 300-600), a PI-certified 200 bar supply tank + tank regulator (~USD 300-600 combined), 2x shuttle valves (~USD 100-250 each, per the Fluido-Sistem-vs-Lee-Co. data point above), plus custom-machined intensifier/actuator bodies (material cost ~USD 100-400, machining typically absorbed as free university-shop labor rather than costed). Rough total: USD 1,500-3,500 in purchased components for a pneumatic/pneumo-hydraulic EBS, excluding pre-existing brake calipers/pedal box and excluding machine-shop labor. An electromechanical spring-based design would trade pressure-vessel/valve costs for a more powerful motor, holding-driver electronics, and a latch mechanism; no sourced cost estimate exists for that architecture in this corpus.
steering_actuation: Full detail is in the companion item 'Steering Actuation Approaches for Driverless'. Summary: common architectures are (a) BLDC motor + planetary gearbox + inline ball screw acting on the rack (back-drivable, simplifies DT.2.2 decoupling since no clutch is strictly needed - Politecnico di Torino/Squadra Corse SC19); (b) motor + planetary gearbox + synchronous belt drive off-axis from the rack, permitted for autonomous actuators under the 2026 rules' belt exception; (c) rack-parallel ball screw driven by a brushless servo motor mounted directly at the rack, ~0.4 s lock-to-lock and ~2000 N at the rack (a pattern seen across several teams in this project's broader research); (d) a linear actuator engaging via a pneumatic clamp orthogonal to the column (Chalmers' original design), found to suffer clamp play causing measurable 'steering reduction' versus commanded angle - the team's own thesis recommended replacing it with a motor-and-pinion rack-and-pinion system; (e) emerging integrated quasi-direct-drive actuator modules (e.g. CubeMars AK-series) mounted directly at the column/rack, eliminating a separate gearbox stage.
brake_actuation: For normal (non-emergency) autonomous driving, two patterns are documented: (1) pure regenerative braking with the EBS hardware used only as a binary on/off emergency actuator, never for graduated deceleration (this project's broader team research found AMZ using this pattern); (2) the same pneumo-hydraulic intensifier hardware used for BOTH normal service braking (at a regulated, lower, dosed pressure) and emergency braking (at full pressure) - the FSAE Driverless Systems Form example BOM includes a labeled 'QM2' valve described in the FSG reference guide as potentially 'a pressure control valve for dosed braking', consistent with sharing hardware between the DSB (DT.3.1, which per DT.3.1.1.c 'may be part of the hydraulic brake system') and the EBS. [uncertain] which pattern is more common across the broader team population, since most teams in this project's prior research did not disclose which they use.
sensor_mounting_packaging: EBS-specific packaging constraints from the rules: all EBS parts (per DT.3.1.1.a) must sit inside the Rollover Protection Envelope; Deactivation Points (DT.3.1.2.b) must be mounted inside the DT.2.3 sensor/AS volume and located either near the DSMS or on the top side of the vehicle between the Front Bulkhead and Front Hoop close to the centerline, near each other, and protected from being struck by a cone while driving. The FSG reference guide adds practical packaging guidance: all mechanical/hydraulic/pneumatic EBS parts should be easily accessible without excessive disassembly, properly attached, and pneumatic cylinders specifically must avoid lateral-force introduction via anti-blocking slots or a swivel mount to the chassis.
mass_added: [uncertain] No team in this corpus published a total EBS+steering-actuator mass-added figure. Order-of-magnitude estimate synthesized from the component classes identified (pressure tanks, valves, brackets, shuttle valves, custom intensifier/actuator bodies for EBS; motor, gearbox/ball-screw, mounting bracket for steering): roughly 1-3 kg for a pneumatic/pneumo-hydraulic EBS system and 2-5 kg for a steering actuator assembly, i.e. an estimated combined 3-8 kg added versus a stock EV chassis. This is a synthesized estimate, not a sourced figure.
chassis_impact: Documented/typical impacts: pedal-box redesign to accept the EBS actuator via one of three interfaces (direct pedal actuation, added second master cylinder, or a custom pressure-transducer) - each requiring different bracket engineering; balance-bar repartition must be re-verified (kept at 50:50 in the one documented case) once the EBS taps into the existing hydraulic circuit; the Deactivation Point location constraint (near DSMS or front-bulkhead/hoop centerline) commonly drives a new nosecone/dash bracket; steering actuator integration typically requires a new mounting bracket at the rack end or column, and in at least one documented case (Chalmers) a full redesign of the steering-to-rack coupling was recommended after in-service play/backlash was discovered.
compute_platform: N/A as a general compute-platform field for this item, but relevant detail: KTH's ISO 26262 safety analysis found that a fully compliant EBS Supervisor implementation would require an additional dedicated CPU plus input/output signal verification separate from the main autonomy compute stack; the team chose not to implement this due to resource constraints. The FSG reference architecture (Figure 6) similarly shows a dedicated 'CPU for monitoring' with duplicated power stages, distinct from the main perception/planning compute. Steering actuator control commonly runs on a dedicated motor controller (e.g. in Cyclic Synchronous Torque mode, per the Politecnico di Torino EPS thesis) rather than the main autonomy compute.
sensor_suite: EBS-relevant sensors identified: dual hydraulic-line pressure sensors (example: Variohm EPT3100, up to 250 bar) monitored continuously per DT.3.1.3.b; pneumatic tank/supply pressure sensors (example: FESTO SPTE-P10R-S6-B-2.5K, up to 15 bar); RES (Remote Emergency System) state via CAN as part of the continuous monitoring set. Steering-relevant sensors: dual potentiometers/encoders at both the actuator and the steering rack for redundant, cross-checked angle feedback (method demonstrated in the Chalmers thesis, which compared sent steering requests against potentiometer readings at both locations to diagnose the clamp-play defect).
power_budget: [uncertain] No team published a combined EBS+steering power-draw figure. EBS load is dominated by the continuous coil current of the armed solenoid valve(s) (a few watts class per FESTO MHE2-class valve, with a higher momentary switching current) plus the monitoring CPU/power-stage electronics. Steering actuator load is dominated by motor current during lock-to-lock moves; the closest sourced figure is from an EPS (power-assist, not full autonomous actuator) design using a Maxon EC 60 Flat rated at 150 W continuous, which gives a rough order-of-magnitude for a similarly-sized full autonomous actuator, though a dedicated autonomous steering actuator sized for the full lock-to-lock authority (rather than driver-assist torque) would likely draw more.
shutdown_circuit_implementation: Per DT.4 and the FSG reference design (Figure 6): the EBS Relay and a Redundant EBS system are supplied directly and without delay from GLVMS, DSMS, the Remote Stop Relay, and the EBS Relay itself; two independent power stages (Power Stage 1 and 2) each independently control/monitor an EBS actuation path so that either can hold or release the brakes. A documented 16-step Startup Check routine (FSG guide Section 9.3) exercises this before allowing transition to 'AS Ready': toggling and verifying a watchdog, confirming EBS energy-storage fill and brake-pressure build-up, then individually disabling each of the two EBS actuators in turn while confirming the other still holds pressure, before re-enabling both and transitioning to Ready. Continuous monitoring during operation (DT.3.1.3.b) tracks pneumatic tank pressure, brake-line pressure, valve mechanical state, sensor plausibility, the brake transfer function, and RES state via CAN.
remote_stop_system: Per DT.3.3 and the FSG reference: the standard Remote Stop System (Vehicle Module + Control Box + Remote Stop Relay) opens the Shutdown Circuit when its Stop Button is pressed, which per DT.3.2.2.b (electrical power loss at the EBS) triggers the Emergency Brake Maneuver. Loss of RES signal/range is itself cited as a documented EBS-triggering event in KTH's data-logger discussion ('EBS is activated due to range loss of the RES'). No team-specific sourcing/integration cost or lead-time detail for the RES hardware itself was found in this pass; the standard RES kit is centrally specified by the competition rather than team-sourced.
status_indicators: N/A / not the focus of this item. Only noted in passing: activation of the EBS corresponds to the 'AS Emergency' Driverless System Status (per the FSG reference guide), which per DT.1.3/DT.1.4 must be reflected in the DSSI/ASSI status lights and alert sound; no EBS-specific indicator hardware/cost/lead-time detail was found.
custom_pcbs: [uncertain] The FSAE Driverless Systems Form example BOM lists the EBS actuator itself (a pressure transducer) as a 'Self-built' mechanical part, and the FSG reference architecture (Figure 6) shows a custom monitoring/power-stage board ('CPU for monitoring' + dual power stages), but no source in this pass gives a fab/bring-up duration or cost for that board specifically.
software_stack: N/A - this item covers the EBS hardware/mechanical subsystem; see EBS Supervisor state-machine notes under shutdown_circuit_implementation and control_approach.
ros_version: N/A - not applicable to EBS hardware; EBS Supervisor logic in the sources reviewed runs as embedded/state-machine firmware, not a ROS node.
perception_approach: N/A - not applicable to this subsystem.
slam_localization_approach: N/A - not applicable to this subsystem.
planning_approach: N/A - not applicable to this subsystem.
control_approach: EBS control is a monitored open-loop trigger, not a continuous control loop: an armed/passive energy store is released on trigger (loss of the relevant relay signal), with a state machine handling Startup Check, continuous monitoring, arm, actuate, and release phases (demonstrated end-to-end in the Politecnico di Torino thesis 16284's state-machine simulation and bench test, including a documented dual-MOSFET check sequence that individually disables each of the two EBS lines to confirm redundant capability). This is distinct from the steering actuator's control loop, which in the closest documented power-assist example (Politecnico di Torino EPS thesis) uses a torque-mode (Cyclic Synchronous Torque) control law on the motor controller with a Linear Quadratic model of resisting friction/self-aligning torque.
simulation_tooling: The only simulation tooling explicitly documented for this subsystem is a Simulink model used to compute motor resisting-torque/self-aligning-moment behavior for steering-torque sizing (Politecnico di Torino EPS thesis), and a software-in-the-loop state-machine simulation of a full EBS arm/check/actuate/release mission cycle prior to hardware bring-up (Politecnico di Torino thesis 16284). No dedicated EBS physical/pneumatic simulation tool (e.g. a hydraulic-circuit simulator) was cited by name in any source reviewed.
ci_cd_testing: N/A - not documented for this hardware subsystem in the sources reviewed; see validation_strategy for the bench/vehicle test sequence actually used.
data_logging: The FSAE Driverless Systems Form requires a CAN DBC file (DSF.8) covering all EBS/RES-relevant signals, and the FSG reference guide notes the data logger's purpose is specifically to reconstruct EBS-triggering events (e.g. 'EBS is activated due to range loss of the RES') after the fact - i.e. EBS/RES signals are treated as first-class items in the mandated logging set, distinct from general perception/planning telemetry.
open_source_repos: [uncertain] None of the primary theses/reference documents reviewed for this item are themselves public code repositories. One adjacent example from this project's broader team research (QUT Motorsport) is reported to maintain dedicated 'steering_actuator' and EBS-test-mission ROS2 packages in a public GitHub org, but the exact repository URL was not captured in this research pass and is not re-cited here to avoid an unverified link.
critical_path_items: Top 3 across sources: (1) procurement of a certified (PI/TPED-class) pressure tank and matching regulator - both a genuine long-lead item and a paperwork item (5-year service-life expiry, transport-certification marking called out explicitly in the FSG reference guide); (2) design/manufacture of the custom pneumatic-to-hydraulic intensifier or direct actuator body - a bespoke, iterated part in every implementation found (the Politecnico di Torino thesis pair each independently re-derives actuator sizing from scratch, suggesting this step is not easily reused year-to-year); (3) integration into the existing hydraulic brake circuit without disturbing brake balance - requires re-verifying balance-bar repartition and adds a shuttle-valve plumbing step documented as consuming significant design iteration in both Politecnico di Torino theses.
long_lead_procurement: [uncertain] No source gives a directly-measured procurement lead time in weeks; the following are inferred from component class/sourcing channel and should be treated as estimates only: certified (PI/TPED) pressure tanks and regulators - est. 4-8 weeks, given the certification/paperwork overhead the FSG guide flags; custom pneumo-hydraulic intensifiers (e.g. Fluido-Sistem-style bespoke parts) - est. 6-10 weeks as a custom-manufactured, non-catalog item; premium industrial motion components (Maxon BLDC motors, Bosch Rexroth ball screws, used in the steering actuator) - est. 4-8 weeks as catalog-but-made-to-order industrial items; motorsport-catalog brake hardware (AP Racing shuttle valves, master cylinders) - est. 2-6 weeks; COTS integrated actuator modules (e.g. CubeMars AK-series quasi-direct-drive units) - est. 1-3 weeks domestically, longer if shipped internationally from the primary Chinese suppliers.
first_static_test_date: N/A - not a team-history field for this item. See validation_strategy for the typical bench-then-static-then-dynamic test sequence.
first_dynamic_test_date: N/A - not a team-history field for this item. See validation_strategy for the typical bench-then-static-then-dynamic test sequence.
testing_hours_before_first_comp: [uncertain] No aggregate testing-hours figure was found. The FSG reference guide's advice to design the system so 'multiple EBS tests in a row' can be performed, or so it can be 'quickly refilled', implies scrutineering-day testing alone commonly involves 5-15+ actuations per team, separate from and in addition to whatever off-season bench/rig testing was done (which is unquantified in every source reviewed).
validation_strategy: Synthesized typical sequence across sources: (1) component-level bench test of individual valves/sensors/intensifiers; (2) subassembly bench test of the full pneumatic/hydraulic circuit on a rig simulating brake-line loads, explicitly including a simulated single-line failure to demonstrate DT.3.2.5.c half-performance (documented: one implementation reached ~40 bar full-line and ~20 bar single-line-failure on the bench); (3) software-in-the-loop state-machine simulation of a full mission's EBS arm/check/actuate/release cycle before hardware is even connected; (4) vehicle-jacked-up static test of the Startup Check routine (documented 16-step example in the FSG reference guide); (5) low-speed dynamic testing building up progressively to the full ~40 km/h DI.2-equivalent profile; (6) the scrutineering EBS test itself, for which multiple attempts/requeues are explicitly anticipated by the FSG reference guide. Steering actuator validation observed separately: bench comparison of commanded vs. measured angle via potentiometers/encoders at both the actuator and the rack (the method that surfaced the Chalmers clamp-play defect), followed by progressive on-vehicle testing at restricted speed per general FS driverless guidance.
rules_compliance_challenges: DT.3.2.1.a ('only passive systems with mechanical energy storage') rules out any EBS concept relying on live electrical actuation alone, forcing every design toward stored spring/gas/hydraulic energy; DT.3.2.5.c ('half performance on single failure') forces full duplication of tanks/valves/sensing/lines, directly shaping component selection (e.g. the Politecnico di Torino cost/weight trade-off between a EUR 100 and a EUR 420 shuttle valve, needed x2) and roughly doubling the already-tight cockpit packaging problem; DT.3.1.2's Deactivation Point constraints (max 2 points, located near the DSMS or the front-bulkhead/hoop centerline, marked 'Brake Release', red handle, max 2 simple actions, must work without electrical power) force early nosecone/dash layout decisions; DT.2.2's actuator-decoupling requirements ('no parts removed', 'must not block manual operation in any position', 'securely locked in the two positions') push steering actuator design toward back-drivable ball-screw or clutch-based mechanisms rather than simple bolt-on/off mounts, since a fully-removable mount would violate 'no parts removed'.
tech_inspection_experience: Repurposed as typical/common cross-team experience: the FSG reference guide itself warns 'there will be limited time for each inspection slot. If it takes too long to sufficiently test the system you will need to requeue', implying a first-attempt pass is not the default expectation and teams commonly plan for re-attempts. A documented failure case from this project's broader team research (QUT Motorsport, Dec 2024): a car whose EBS logic had existed and passed checks since mid-2022 nonetheless crashed during the live EBS dynamic test when a path-computation delay caused a sharp steering correction at ~40 km/h just before the finish line, sending the car into a wall/tyre barrier; both remote stop and EBS were triggered but could not fully arrest the vehicle before impact. This illustrates that EBS-test failure is not always an EBS-hardware problem - a control-software timing fault in the preceding acceleration phase (DI.2.2.2.a, accelerate to 40 km/h in <=20 m) can cause a failure that looks like an EBS failure.
ebs_test_experience: The DI.2 Emergency Brake System Test (per FSAE_Driverless_2026_V4 DI.2) requires: accelerate in Driverless Mode to >=40 km/h within <=20 m; the Remote Stop is triggered at a specific point; the vehicle must then stop within <=8.5 m (scalable by officials on a wet track); conducted after the rest of Technical Inspection is complete. Common failure modes identified across sources: (a) insufficient deceleration/stopping distance from under-pressurized, leaking, or improperly sized lines - directly why the rules floor of >10 m/s2 average deceleration (DT.3.2.5.b) and the actuation-time-derated force sizing (see top_mistakes) exist; (b) reaction time exceeding the 200 ms cap (DT.3.2.5.a) from slow valve/relay switching - one thesis explicitly targets 150 ms of margin under the cap in its actuator sizing; (c) directional instability/yaw during braking violating the 'stable driving condition' requirement (DT.3.2.5.d); (d) control-software timing/perception errors during the preceding 40 km/h acceleration phase causing loss of path tracking before the brake event even starts (documented QUT crash, see tech_inspection_experience); (e) RES/remote-stop trigger-timing edge cases - since DI.2.2.2.b specifies the Remote Stop 'starts at a specific point', misjudging that trigger point relative to the 20 m acceleration zone is a plausible and commonly-discussed source of over/under-shoot, though no source gives a numeric fail-rate for this specific cause.
documentation_burden: The Driverless Systems Form (DSF) imposes an EBS-specific documentation package beyond the general Engineering Design Report: a Pressure System Overview diagram (DSF.5) using DIN ISO 1219 symbols covering EVERY pneumatic/hydraulic component with no simplification allowed (DSF.5.1.1) and justification that tank volume is sufficient for the required energy (DSF.5.2.7); an Actuator Power Supply Schematic (DSF.2); a Continuous Monitoring Flowchart (DSF.3); a High-Level Block Diagram (DSF.4); a Startup Checks Flowchart (DSF.6); Mechanical Assembly Drawings for all self-built pressure-system parts (DSF.7.1.2); and a CAN DBC file (DSF.8). The FSG reference guide frames this documentation as existing partly to speed up technical inspection itself, implying teams that under-invest in it pay a time cost at scrutineering, not just in report scoring.
autonomous_speeds_achieved: N/A as team-specific results, but note: the DI.2 test standardizes the target speed at exactly 40 km/h minimum, reached within 20 m, as the common reference point used across the corpus for EBS actuation-force and reaction-time sizing calculations.
ebs_deceleration_achieved: Rule floor (DT.3.2.5): reaction time <=200 ms, average deceleration >10 m/s2, half of that performance acceptable on a single failure. No source in this pass reports a directly MEASURED on-track deceleration/reaction-time pair for a completed vehicle. Closest documented figures: the Politecnico di Torino design thesis (18714) targets/calculates a 150 ms actuation time (within the 200 ms cap) for a hydraulic pull-type actuator sized for 1.8 g (~17.7 m/s2) design deceleration, applying a 60% load-factor derating specifically because high-speed (200 ms) actuation reduces achievable hydraulic actuator force; the companion implementation thesis (16284) bench-validated ~40 bar full-line / ~20 bar single-line-failure hydraulic pressure but reports no vehicle-measured deceleration, since vehicle testing was not completed within the thesis. This is a genuine gap in the public corpus - no verified on-track EBS performance number was found.
perception_range_achieved: N/A - not applicable to this subsystem.
reliability_notes: Cross-team EBS/steering reliability notes found: QUT Motorsport's Dec 2024 EBS-test crash (root cause: path-computation delay causing a sharp steering correction at 40 km/h, not an EBS-hardware failure per se, but occurring during and disrupting the EBS test scenario, ending the car's competitive career for that season); Chalmers' original pneumatic-clamp linear steering actuator exhibited measurable 'play' causing quantified 'steering reduction' (commanded angle not fully achieved) versus potentiometer-measured actual angle, worse on rough track surfaces - a defect the team's own thesis says was only fully characterized after a season of use via dedicated bench-style testing, not caught earlier in development.
top_mistakes: (1) Sizing the EBS actuator/pressure system around idealized, frictionless, static-force assumptions rather than the FS-relevant actuation-time-derated force: one thesis explicitly applies a 60% load-factor derating because 'due to such high actuation rate[s], hydraulic actuators cannot provide the desired [static-rated] force' within the 200 ms window - a factor easy to miss if sizing only from a static-load datasheet number. (2) Treating DSF/pressure-system documentation (DIN ISO 1219 diagrams, tank-volume justification, mechanical assembly drawings for every self-built part) as a late paperwork add-on rather than designing it in parallel with hardware, when the rules require EVERY component to appear with no simplification (DSF.5.1.1). (3) Choosing an actuator-to-mechanism coupling with backlash/play (a pneumatic-clamp linear actuator, in the one documented case) without early bench validation of commanded-vs-actual angle, only discovering the resulting 'steering reduction' after a full season of on-track use. (4) Treating EBS design as 'done' at the CAD/bench-test stage without budgeting a further multi-month vehicle-integration-and-DI.2-iteration phase - both Politecnico di Torino theses reviewed explicitly stop short of a completed vehicle test, each ending with a 'way forward' section describing the remaining work, which is a recurring thesis-to-competition timeline gap rather than an isolated incident.
advice_for_new_teams: "Design the redundancy in from day one - DT.3.2.5.c (half performance on single failure) is not an add-on, it doubles your valve/tank/line count and should shape packaging from the first CAD iteration" (synthesized from the FSG reference guide's redundancy section and the Politecnico di Torino dual-intensifier architecture). "Budget for the actuation-time derating: because a 200 ms actuation window is mandated, hydraulic actuators cannot deliver their static-rated force, so apply a load-factor derating (one thesis used 60%) when sizing" (Politecnico di Torino thesis 18714). "Make the EBS testable in isolation and quickly re-armable, because scrutineering gives you a limited slot and you may need several attempts in a row" (FSG reference guide Section 9.6). "Validate the actuator-to-mechanism coupling on a bench rig, comparing commanded vs. measured angle/position, before trusting it on-track - backlash or clamp play that looks negligible on the bench can show up as a measurable performance defect after a season of real driving" (Chalmers thesis finding).

recruiting_and_knowledge_transfer: [uncertain] Not directly documented for this subsystem across teams. One structural observation: because several of the richest sources here are university master's/bachelor's theses (KTH, Politecnico di Torino x4, Chalmers), the thesis-driven development model itself functions as a form of built-in knowledge transfer - each design cycle produces a citable, detailed written document, which is unusual compared to software subsystems that typically rely on git history/tribal knowledge. The tradeoff is that this cadence is tied to the academic thesis calendar (roughly one year per thesis) rather than the team's competition calendar, which may partly explain why none of the theses reviewed span a full concept-to-competition-pass cycle.
budget_estimate: [uncertain] Repurposed as: typical EBS+steering-actuator hardware budget, synthesized (not a single sourced total, since no team published one): EBS pneumatic/pneumo-hydraulic system roughly USD 1,500-3,500 in purchased components (see ebs_cost_estimate for the component-level breakdown), excluding pre-existing brake hardware and machine-shop labor; steering actuator roughly USD 800-2,500 for a motor+gearbox/ball-screw build using premium industrial components (Maxon-class motors, Bosch Rexroth ball screws), or roughly USD 300-600 for a single COTS quasi-direct-drive actuator module (CubeMars AK-class) excluding controller/encoder integration labor. Combined typical hardware spend: roughly USD 2,500-6,000.
recommended_sequence: (1) Study DT.3/DT.2 rules text and the DSF pressure-system documentation template BEFORE any CAD, so the diagram/documentation requirement shapes the design rather than following it. (2) Choose architecture (direct pneumatic vs. pneumo-hydraulic intensifier vs. electromechanical spring) based on whether the team already has a working hydraulic service-brake system to piggyback on (true for nearly every EV conversion) - default to a pneumatic or pneumo-hydraulic-intensifier design on the existing hydraulics, and reserve the electromechanical-spring approach for teams specifically wanting to avoid pressure-vessel certification overhead. (3) Size actuator force/stroke using the 200 ms-actuation load-factor-derated force, not the static-rated force. (4) Source the certified pressure tank + regulator EARLY given certification/lead-time risk. (5) Build and bench-test the pressure/valve subassembly standalone, explicitly including a simulated single-line failure. (6) Implement and bench-test the EBS Startup Check + continuous-monitoring state machine in software before vehicle integration. (7) Integrate into vehicle brake lines and re-verify brake balance is undisturbed. (8) Run a static (jacked-up) full-sequence test. (9) Run progressive low-speed dynamic tests, ramping to the full ~40 km/h DI.2 profile. (10) Iterate through scrutineering EBS-test attempts, planning for more than one attempt. In parallel for steering: (1) compute static/dynamic steering torque from tie-rod geometry and a target lock-to-lock time; (2) choose a motor+transmission architecture matching that torque/speed/backlash budget, favoring a back-drivable ball screw to simplify DT.2.2 decoupling; (3) bench-validate commanded-vs-actual angle before vehicle mounting; (4) implement and verify the DT.2.2 decoupling mechanism in both locked positions.
applicability_to_24_month_ramp: For a team with a running EV, ~9 software-focused members, and a 24-month window (June 2026-June 2028): EBS and steering actuation are hardware/mechanical-heavy subsystems that a software-heavy team will under-resource by default. Recommend dedicating at least 1-2 mechanical/mechatronics-focused members to EBS+steering specifically, starting in month 1-3 (rules study + architecture choice), targeting a bench-validated EBS and steering actuator by month 9-12 (consistent with the ~6-9 month bench-validation figure synthesized from the corpus), and reserving month 12-18 for vehicle integration plus iteration through the EBS dynamic test, leaving month 18-24 as schedule margin - the corpus shows that even a well-resourced, multi-year academic program (Politecnico di Torino/Squadra Corse, four separate theses touching EBS/steering/RES across 2019-2021) needed more than one full design-and-build cycle to progress from concept to a fully vehicle-validated system, so a single 24-month first attempt should budget generously for iteration rather than assume a single clean pass. Given the software-heavy team composition, favor the pneumo-hydraulic-intensifier or direct-pneumatic-on-existing-hydraulics EBS architecture (reuses existing brake hardware, avoids inventing a novel electromechanical spring/latch mechanism) and a back-drivable ball-screw or COTS quasi-direct-drive steering actuator (avoids designing a custom clutch/decoupling mechanism from scratch), to minimize the amount of genuinely novel mechanical design the team must originate.
